passage.title: The Notches in Elderberry Bridge
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Sunlight slanted through the gaps in the weathered pine siding of Elderberry Creek Bridge as Tessa stepped onto the thick floor planks. Her boots echoed above the rush of cold North Georgia water below. Tessa's grandfather had helped repair this covered bridge fifty years ago. Before he passed his old canvas tool bag to Tessa, he had sketched a rough map of the bridge trusses on the inside flap. Next to the drawing, he had written one line in faded ink: Count where the X-beams cross the king posts.

Tessa shone her flashlight up into the dim rafters where heavy diagonal timbers formed a row of giant X shapes. High along the center oak beam, a row of slanted tally marks had been deeply chiseled into the timber by the original bridge builder. Most walkers thought the marks were random scratches left by a saw. Yet when Tessa looked closer, she saw that the cuts were neat and deliberate. The first post held three short vertical cuts, the second held five, and the third held two.

Her younger brother, Eli, joined her at the middle window and read the numbers aloud as Tessa wrote them down: three, five, two, and four. Eli wondered if the marks recorded how many wagons crossed the creek on opening day. Tessa shook her head and pointed to the wooden pegs, called trunnels, that pinned each diagonal brace together. Every truss section had six pegs in a row. When she matched the carved numbers to the pegs on the fourth post, she noticed that the fourth peg stuck out an inch farther than the rest.

Standing on the low wheel guard, Tessa gripped the fourth oak peg with both hands and gave it a firm twist. With a dry click, a hollow square of wood slid open inside the thick post. Concealed inside the dry slot rested a small copper tube sealed with beeswax. Tessa pried off the cap and unrolled a crisp sheet of linen paper dated 1884.

The paper held the builder's original stress drawings and a list of the local quarry stones used in the creek piers. At the bottom, a note praised the ingenious lattice design that allowed the bridge to flex under heavy loads without iron nails. Tessa and Eli grinned as they slid the tube into their grandfather's tool bag to share with the county historical society. The old builder had left a guide for the next generation to keep the bridge standing strong.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"High along the center oak beam, a row of slanted tally marks had been deeply chiseled into the timber by the original bridge builder."

Based on the structure of this sentence, who or what carved the tally marks?

options.text: The center oak beam pressing against the roof
options.childFeedback: The center oak beam is the wood that got carved ('into the timber')—the beam didn't chisel tally marks into itself!

options.text: Walkers crossing Elderberry Creek with saws
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 says most walkers thought a saw left random scratches, not that walkers crossed the creek carrying saws to carve the beam.

options.text: The original bridge builder
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'had been deeply chiseled into the timber by' tells us that 'the original bridge builder' is the person who carved the slanted tally marks.

options.text: Tessa's younger brother Eli
options.childFeedback: Eli only reads the carved numbers aloud in Paragraph 3; the original bridge builder chiseled them back in 1884.

questions.provingSentenceText: High along the center oak beam, a row of slanted tally marks had been deeply chiseled into the timber by the original bridge builder.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'had been deeply chiseled into the timber by' tells us that 'the original bridge builder' is the person who carved the slanted tally marks.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'a row of slanted tally marks' is the receiver of the action. The true actor performing the chiseling comes after 'by': 'the original bridge builder' (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Look right after 'had been deeply chiseled into the timber by' in Paragraph 2 to see who carved the marks.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Yet when Tessa looked closer, she saw that the cuts were neat and deliberate."

What does the word "deliberate" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: Done on purpose with careful planning
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, 'deliberate' means done on purpose with careful planning. The author contrasts 'neat and deliberate' cuts with the 'random scratches' most walkers assumed they were.

options.text: Covered in thick green moss from the creek
options.childFeedback: The marks are high up on a dry oak rafter inside the covered bridge, not covered in creek moss! 'Deliberate' means carved on purpose.

options.text: Made by accident when a wagon wheel slipped
options.childFeedback: Made by accident is the exact opposite of 'deliberate'! Tessa sees that the cuts were not random accidents, but neat tally marks carved on purpose.

options.text: Too faint for any flashlight beam to illuminate
options.childFeedback: Tessa can see and count every cut clearly with her flashlight in Paragraph 2, so they aren't too faint to see. 'Deliberate' means intentional.

questions.provingSentenceText: Yet when Tessa looked closer, she saw that the cuts were neat and deliberate.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, 'deliberate' means done on purpose with careful planning. The author contrasts 'neat and deliberate' cuts with the 'random scratches' most walkers assumed they were.
questions.parentExplanation: The previous sentence states that most walkers thought the marks were 'random scratches.' The contrast word 'Yet' and the pairing with 'neat' show that 'deliberate' means done on purpose with careful planning (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Contrast 'neat and deliberate' with 'random scratches left by a saw' in the sentence right before it in Paragraph 2.

questions.prompt: How does Tessa figure out which wooden peg to twist in Paragraph 3?

options.text: She counts the number of wagons pictured on the inside flap of her grandfather's tool bag.
options.childFeedback: Her grandfather's tool bag flap in Paragraph 1 held a sketch of bridge trusses, not pictures of wagons! It was Eli who wondered about wagons in Paragraph 3.

options.text: She pulls on every single peg in the bridge until one of them breaks off in her hand.
options.childFeedback: Tessa doesn't pull on every peg or break anything; she uses the tally numbers to go straight to the fourth peg on the fourth post and twists it gently.

options.text: She follows a bright red arrow painted on the floor planks by the county historical society.
options.childFeedback: There is no red arrow painted on the floor! In Paragraph 5, Tessa and Eli plan to share their discovery with the historical society for the first time.

options.text: She matches the carved tally numbers to the rows of pegs and sees the fourth peg on the fourth post sticking out.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, Tessa matches the carved tally numbers (3, 5, 2, 4) to the rows of wooden pegs and spots the fourth peg on the fourth post sticking out an inch farther than the rest.

questions.provingSentenceText: When she matched the carved numbers to the pegs on the fourth post, she noticed that the fourth peg stuck out an inch farther than the rest.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, Tessa matches the carved tally numbers (3, 5, 2, 4) to the rows of wooden pegs and spots the fourth peg on the fourth post sticking out an inch farther than the rest.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 3, Tessa compares the sequence of carved numbers (3, 5, 2, 4) to the rows of wooden pegs and notices that on the fourth post, the fourth peg sticks out an inch farther than the others (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Check the last sentence of Paragraph 3 to see what Tessa notices when she matches the carved numbers to the pegs on the fourth post.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of the grandfather's note at the end of Paragraph 1 in the structure of the story?

options.text: It explains why the county decided to close Elderberry Creek Bridge to cars.
options.childFeedback: The note says 'Count where the X-beams cross the king posts'—it never mentions cars or closing the bridge!

options.text: It gives Tessa the specific clue that launches her search up in the bridge rafters.
options.childFeedback: The grandfather's note at the end of Paragraph 1 ('Count where the X-beams cross the king posts') gives Tessa the exact starting clue that directs her flashlight search in Paragraph 2.

options.text: It warns Tessa and Eli to stay off the bridge because the oak beams are rotting.
options.childFeedback: The oak beams aren't rotting; Paragraph 5 says the bridge is standing strong, and the note invites Tessa to count the beams rather than stay away.

options.text: It reveals the ending of the mystery before Tessa even steps onto the planks.
options.childFeedback: The note only tells Tessa where to start counting; she still has to find the tally marks, match the pegs, and open the hidden slot in Paragraphs 2–4.

questions.provingSentenceText: Next to the drawing, he had written one line in faded ink: Count where the X-beams cross the king posts.
questions.childTip: The grandfather's note at the end of Paragraph 1 ('Count where the X-beams cross the king posts') gives Tessa the exact starting clue that directs her flashlight search in Paragraph 2.
questions.parentExplanation: Structurally, the grandfather's clue at the end of Paragraph 1 ('Count where the X-beams cross the king posts') serves as the inciting clue that directs Tessa's investigation in Paragraphs 2 and 3 (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Look at how the ink note at the end of Paragraph 1 tells Tessa where to shine her flashlight at the start of Paragraph 2.

questions.prompt: PART A: Which statement best expresses a central theme of the passage?

options.text: Hidden treasure chests full of gold coins can be found inside every covered bridge in Georgia.
options.childFeedback: Tessa doesn't find gold coins! She finds a copper tube holding 1884 stress drawings and a list of quarry stones to help repair the bridge.

options.text: Old wooden bridges should be torn down and replaced with modern steel highways.
options.childFeedback: The story celebrates preserving the historic 1884 covered bridge and praises its clever wooden lattice design, not tearing it down for steel highways.

options.text: Careful observation can uncover the wisdom that past builders left behind to help future generations preserve their work.
options.childFeedback: By looking closely at tally marks that others brushed off as random scratches, Tessa uncovers the 1884 builder's plans left behind to help future generations care for the bridge.

options.text: Younger brothers are better at solving math codes than older sisters.
options.childFeedback: Eli helps read the numbers aloud, but Tessa is the one who figures out that the numbers match the wooden pegs on the trusses.

questions.provingSentenceText: The old builder had left a guide for the next generation to keep the bridge standing strong.
questions.childTip: By looking closely at tally marks that others brushed off as random scratches, Tessa uncovers the 1884 builder's plans left behind to help future generations care for the bridge.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RL2, the story's theme centers on intergenerational stewardship: by looking closely where others saw only random scratches, Tessa recovers the 1884 engineering plans left to help future generations care for the bridge (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Think about what Tessa's careful observation uncovered in Paragraph 5 and why the old builder left those drawings behind.

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "The old builder had left a guide for the next generation to keep the bridge standing strong."
options.childFeedback: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by explaining that the 1884 builder hid his drawings as a guide for future generations to keep the bridge strong.

options.text: "Most walkers thought the marks were random scratches left by a saw."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 2 only shows that most walkers missed the clue, without showing the wisdom the builder left for future generations.

options.text: "Eli wondered if the marks recorded how many wagons crossed the creek on opening day."
options.childFeedback: This line from Paragraph 3 only shares Eli's incorrect guess about the tally marks before Tessa solves the peg puzzle.

options.text: "Her boots echoed above the rush of cold North Georgia water below."
options.childFeedback: This opening detail from Paragraph 1 only describes the sound of Tessa's boots above the creek, not the theme of preserving past wisdom.

questions.provingSentenceText: The old builder had left a guide for the next generation to keep the bridge standing strong.
questions.childTip: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by explaining that the 1884 builder hid his drawings as a guide for future generations to keep the bridge strong.
questions.parentExplanation: Option D directly supports the theme in Part A by stating how the hidden 1884 stress drawings connect past craftsmanship with the next generation's preservation efforts.
